title_en: Oration on the Inscriptions of the Psalms of Ascents
author: Eustathius of Antioch
occasion: The surviving fragments explain the titles of the Psalms of Ascents, focusing on why acquired glory is not fitting for the Father or the Word, but rather for the man of Christ who is raised from the dead, and the subsequent shaming and scattering of Christ's enemies.
argument: The Father does not receive acquired glory, since he is perfect, infinite, incomprehensible, and without need of beauty and every seemliness. Nor does the Word, who is God begotten from the Father and through whom all created things were made. Rather, it is the man of Christ who is raised from the dead, exalted, and glorified, while the opponents openly took up shame. Those who took up hatred against him out of envy and were fenced in by hostile battle-line are scattered, the Word and God having fittingly raised up his own temple.

outline.move: The Father does not receive acquired glory, being perfect, infinite, incomprehensible, and without need of beauty and every seemliness.

The Word as God begotten from the Father and creator of all things is also not the recipient of acquired glory; instead the man of Christ, raised from the dead, is exalted and glorified, while the opponents took up shame openly.

The opponents openly took up shame; those who took up hatred against him out of envy and were fenced in by hostile battle-line are scattered, the Word and God having fittingly raised up his own temple.

cast.name: Father
cast.who: God the Father, described as perfect, infinite, incomprehensible, and without need of beauty and every seemliness.

cast.name: Word
cast.who: God begotten from the Father, through whom all created things were made.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: The anointed one whose man is raised from the dead and glorified. Note: The Greek speaks of 'the man of Christ' (ὁ ἄνθρωπος τοῦ Χριστοῦ), not 'the humanity of Christ'—a theologically significant distinction in Eustathius's anti-Arian Christology.

key_terms.sense: Glory that is acquired or added from outside, as opposed to inherent divine glory.
The man of Christ, distinguished from the divine Word; the human being who is raised from the dead and glorified.
The divine Word, God begotten from the Father and agent of creation.
The temple, here referring to Christ's body which the Word raises.
Raising up, used of the resurrection of Christ's body by the Word and God.
The adversaries or enemies of Christ who are put to shame.

scripture: The work comments on the Psalms of Ascents (Psalms 119-133 in the Septuagint numbering, corresponding to Psalms 120-134 in the Hebrew numbering). Citations should follow the Septuagint Psalm numbering used by the author.
uncertain: The exact date of composition within Eustathius's lifetime.
The original addressee or audience of the work.
The complete structure and scope of the original treatise, since only fragments survive.
